Uzbekistan is the jewel of the Silk Road: turquoise domes, ancient madrasas and legendary cities that look much as they did five centuries ago, in a safe, halal, visa-free country four hours from the Gulf. Here are the best things to do in Uzbekistan for your 2026 trip, with practical detail on timing, tickets and what suits families.

1. Registan Square, Samarkand

The most iconic sight in Central Asia: three majestic madrasas (Ulugh Beg from 1420, Sher-Dor and Tilya-Kori from the 1600s) framing a vast square covered in intricate blue tilework. Visit twice: in the morning when the light hits the eastern facade, and after sunset for the illumination. Climb the minaret for the view, see the gold-leaf interior of Tilya-Kori, and stay for the evening light show in summer. Allow two to three hours; tickets are a few dollars.

2. The Old City of Bukhara

A living museum of 2,000 years: the Poi Kalon ensemble with its 47-metre minaret that even Genghis Khan spared, the Ark fortress, the covered trading domes still selling carpets and knives, and the Lyabi-Hauz pool surrounded by tea houses. Bukhara is best explored on foot over two days, with an evening stroll when the lanes empty. Stay in a converted merchant house inside the old city.

3. Khiva's Itchan Kala

A complete walled city of mud-brick walls, palaces and the unfinished turquoise Kalta Minor minaret, car-free and compact. One combined ticket covers most monuments. The best moment is sunset from the city walls or the Islam Khoja minaret. Reach it by domestic flight to Urgench (40 minutes from Tashkent) or the six-hour desert drive from Bukhara with a stop at the ancient Khorezm fortresses.

4. Tashkent, the modern capital

Start or end the trip here: the Hazrati Imam complex holding one of the world's oldest Qurans, the domed Chorsu Bazaar for dried fruit and bread, the metro with its chandelier-lit stations, and Magic City park for children. Tashkent also has the international hotels, the best restaurants and the Afrosiyob high-speed train to Samarkand (two hours).

5. Shah-i-Zinda, Samarkand

A narrow avenue of mausoleums from the 11th to 15th centuries, each facade more intricate than the last, climbing the hill above Samarkand. It is the most photographed corner of Uzbekistan and a place of pilgrimage; dress modestly and go early to avoid the groups. Combine with the nearby Bibi-Khanym Mosque and Siyob Bazaar.

6. The shrine of Imam al-Bukhari and other pilgrimage sites

For Muslim travellers, Uzbekistan is also a pilgrimage: the mausoleum of Imam al-Bukhari near Samarkand, the shrine of Baha-ud-Din Naqshband outside Bukhara, and the Imam al-Tirmidhi complex in Termez. Our guides arrange visits with time for prayer; see why Uzbekistan.

7. Silk Road crafts and cuisine

Watch silk being woven in Margilan, ceramics painted in Rishtan and paper made from mulberry bark in Konigil village near Samarkand; children can try each craft. Eat plov cooked in a giant kazan at the Tashkent Plov Centre, samsa from a clay oven, and the sweet melons of Khorezm. All food is halal.

8. The Kyzylkum desert and yurt camps

Between Bukhara and Khiva, a night in a yurt camp near Lake Aydarkul with camel rides, a campfire and desert stars is the highlight of many family trips; best in April, May, September and October.

Suggested itineraries

  • 5 days: Tashkent (1), Samarkand (2), Bukhara (2).
  • 7 days: adds Khiva or a yurt night; see the 7-day Uzbekistan program.
  • 10 days: combines Uzbekistan with Almaty in Kazakhstan.

More on each city in the most important tourist cities in Uzbekistan and the Samarkand guide.

Best time to visit Uzbekistan

April to early June and September to early November: 20–30°C, clear skies, and Nowruz (21 March) or the Silk and Spices Festival (late May) as bonuses. July exceeds 40°C in Bukhara and Khiva; if you must travel in summer, sightsee early and late and choose a hotel with a pool. Winter is cold, cheap and uncrowded. See the best time for family travel.

Practical notes

  • GCC citizens enter visa-free for 30 days; most other nationalities get an e-visa online.
  • Book Afrosiyob train seats and Bukhara boutique hotels early in spring and autumn.
  • Cards work in hotels and larger restaurants; carry som for bazaars.
  • A family of four spends roughly 2,200–3,400 USD for a week on a private program, excluding flights.
